title: 28 — Design a Stock Exchange
html:
28 — Design a Stock Exchange

The one idea: an exchange is a deterministic, sequenced state machine. Orders are stamped with sequence numbers by a sequencer, fed to a single-threaded in-memory matching engine per symbol, and every input and output is logged so the whole state can be replayed. Latency comes from keeping the critical path on one machine, avoiding network hops, locks and garbage.

Step 1 — Scope

  • Trading stocks only; place limit orders; cancel orders; real-time market data (order book, trades).
  • 100 symbols, 1 billion orders/day; trading hours 6.5 h.
  • Risk checks (e.g. max 1M shares of a symbol per user per day); wallet checks (sufficient funds).
  • Very high availability; fault tolerance; low, predictable latency (millisecond → microsecond); security (KYC, DDoS).

Estimates: 1B ÷ (6.5 × 3,600) ≈ ~43,000 orders/s, peak ~215,000/s (open/close spikes).

Trading 101

Term Meaning
Broker Client-facing firm that routes orders to the exchange
Limit order Buy/sell at a fixed price or better
Market order Execute immediately at the prevailing price
Order book Per-symbol list of resting buy (bids) and sell (asks) orders by price level
Level 1/2/3 data Best bid/ask / price-level depths / individual order depths
Candlestick Open, high, low, close per interval
FIX Financial Information eXchange protocol

Step 2 — High-level design

Three flows:

---
title: Stock exchange — trading critical path
---
flowchart LR
    B["Broker"] -->|FIX| CG["Client gateway<br/>(auth, validation, rate limit)"]
    CG --> OM["Order manager<br/>(risk check, wallet check)"]
    OM --> SQ1["Sequencer<br/>(inbound)"]
    SQ1 --> ME["Matching engine<br/>(order book per symbol)"]
    ME --> SQ2["Sequencer<br/>(outbound executions)"]
    SQ2 --> OM
    OM --> CG
    ME --> MDP["Market data publisher"] --> DS["Data service"] --> B
    SQ2 --> Rep["Reporter"] --> DB[("Reporting DB")]

Critical path (trading flow)

gateway → order manager → sequencer → matching engine → sequencer → order manager → gateway. Everything else is off the critical path.

  • Client gateway: thin — authentication, validation, rate limiting, normalisation. Colocated with brokers for the fastest clients.
  • Order manager: risk checks, wallet (fund withholding), state of each order; sends to the sequencer.
  • Sequencer: stamps monotonic sequence IDs on every inbound order and outbound execution → deterministic ordering, gap detection, replayability. It is both the ordering authority and the durable log.
  • Matching engine: maintains the order book per symbol, matches buys against sells (price-time priority / FIFO), emits executions (fills). Must be deterministic — same input sequence → same output.
  • Market data publisher: builds order book depth and candlestick charts from executions, publishes to subscribers.
  • Reporter: collects executions for reporting, reconciliation, tax, compliance — not latency sensitive.

Order book data structure

Per symbol: two sides; each side a sorted map of price level → FIFO queue of orders. Needs:

  • Add at a price level: O(1) (append to queue).
  • Match at best price: O(1).
  • Cancel by order ID: O(1) → keep a orderId → node map and use a doubly linked list per level.

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 Performance: the critical path on one server

Latency = Σ (network hops + disk I/O + processing). Remove hops and disk:

  • Put gateway-side components, order manager, sequencer and matching engine on one server, communicating via an mmap-ed shared-memory event store (ring buffer), not the network.
  • Application loop: each component is a single thread pinned to a CPU core, busy-polling its queue — no locks, no context switches, predictable latency.
  • Avoid GC pauses (object pooling, preallocated arrays); avoid disk I/O on the hot path (mmap files flushed by the OS).
  • This gives tens of microseconds end to end.

3.2 Event sourcing

All inputs and outputs are events in the append-only store: NewOrderEvent, OrderFilledEvent… The order manager and matching engine rebuild state by replaying events — the same pattern as chapter 27, applied for determinism and recovery.

3.3 High availability

  • Run a hot-warm pair: the warm matching engine consumes the same event stream and processes it, but doesn't emit. On primary failure (heartbeats), warm takes over — recovering in seconds.
  • Replicate the event store across machines with Raft (reliable UDP multicast between servers) — leader election gives automatic failover across DCs.
  • RTO in seconds, RPO near zero.

3.4 Fairness

Market data must reach all subscribers at the same time — multicast over reliable UDP; colocation services sold equally; order of processing strictly by sequence number.

3.5 Market data

Candlestick charts in memory with ring buffers; keep recent data hot, persist historical data to a columnar store.

3.6 Network security

DDoS protection: isolate public services, cache read-only data, harden URLs, allowlist/blocklist, and rate limit.

Step 4 — Wrap-up

Sequencer + deterministic single-threaded matching engine per symbol, event sourcing for replay, everything on one box on the critical path, hot-warm with Raft for HA, multicast for fair market data. Modern exchanges increasingly run on the cloud with this same architecture for non-latency-critical venues (crypto exchanges); AMM (automated market makers) are a DeFi alternative.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • Order book in C#: SortedDictionary<decimal, LinkedList<Order>> per side (bids ordered descending via a custom comparer) + Dictionary<long, LinkedListNode<Order>> for O(1) cancel. For low latency, replace with preallocated arrays indexed by price tick.
  • Single-writer loop: a dedicated thread (new Thread(..., IsBackground = true)) reading from a bounded System.Threading.Channels channel with SingleReader = true, or an LMAX Disruptor-style ring buffer (Disruptor-net).
  • GC: GCSettings.LatencyMode = GCLatencyMode.SustainedLowLatency, ArrayPool<T>, structs, Span<T> — avoid allocations on the hot path; Native AOT for startup and predictability.
  • Sequencing/replay: an append-only event log (memory-mapped file via MemoryMappedFile) with a monotonic long sequence.
  • FIX protocol: QuickFIX/n.
  • Azure is fine for non-HFT venues and for the off-critical-path parts (reporting → Azure SQL/ADX, market data fan-out → Event Hubs/SignalR); Proximity placement groups and accelerated networking reduce VM-to-VM latency.

Review checklist

  • Trading basics: limit order, order book, price-time priority.
  • Critical path identified and minimised.
  • Sequencer and deterministic matching engine.
  • Order book structure with O(1) cancel.
  • Single-threaded, core-pinned loops; mmap event store; no GC on the hot path.
  • Event sourcing, hot-warm failover, Raft.
  • Fair market data distribution.
